_doc: The Human Baseline - Complete 9-Act Linear Narrative Dialogue Graph with full expanded ensemble cast.

nodes.text: Late Friday afternoon at Pete's Auto Care. The shop is filled with the steady rhythm of three active bays: the hiss of pneumatic lines, the low thrum of the air compressor, and classic rock drifting from a grease-spotted radio on the workbench.
Hand me that three-eighths torque wrench, Pete. Setting tension on this timing belt pulley. Forty-two foot-pounds, right where the service manual calls for it.

Here you go, kid. Calibrated yesterday. Don't go stripping the aluminum threads on Pete's watch—though God knows you've got better feel for bolt tolerances than half the dealership mechanics in this county.

A click sounds as the torque clicks true. Across the service desk, three customer invoices sit neatly in the pickup rack, each stamped 'PAID - CASH/CARD'. In Year Zero, when an engine rolls into the shop, families have the steady income to keep it running.

Good evening, this is Diane Sterling with the 5:00 Business Pulse. State employment figures reached a four-year high this afternoon as regional manufacturing and retail outpace seasonal estimates, driven by steady consumer demand.
Enjoy the numbers while they're green, Todd. When the suits on the television start bragging about peak efficiency, it usually means someone in an office tower is planning a merger.

Phone buzzes on the tool chest. Text from Adriana: 'Truck arrived on time. Five pallets cleared, displays built, all four clerks showed up with energy. We're locking the registers at 7. Don't burn the burgers tonight.'

Todd wipes his hands on a clean red shop rag, rolls down the middle bay door, and clocks out on the analog punch clock. Outside, the early autumn breeze is clean. Across town at Oakridge Liquors, Adriana is wrapping up her floor shift.

Inside the bright, orderly aisles of Oakridge Liquors, the shelves are neatly fronted and faced. Warm amber bottles of Kentucky bourbon gleam under recessed halogen lights as delivery carts roll smoothly over the threshold.
Last case of single barrel stacked on the endcap, boss! Floor is swept, weekend signage is up, and register one is balanced.
Sharp work, Kendra. Take your full thirty-minute break before you head out. Don't let campus classes run you ragged this semester—steady hours, steady sleep.
Thanks, Adriana. You're the only department manager in the whole supermarket chain who doesn't breathe down our necks with stopwatches. See you Monday!

There are no automated cameras tracking Kendra's keystrokes or algorithms shaving minutes off her timecard. Labor is managed with human trust, clear expectations, and mutual respect. Adriana sets the safe alarm, locks the glass entrance, and heads home to the backyard cookout.
The backyard deck smells of hickory charcoal, sizzling beef, and fresh cedar planks. Twilight paints the sky in shades of amber and indigo as bistro string lights glow above the lawn table.
Burgers are off the grates. Sharp cheddar for Marcus, pepper jack for Sam, and Chloe gets the grilled vegetable skewers.

Man, Todd, you're a miracle worker. Speaking of miracles—we just finished our sprint two days ahead of schedule at the tech firm. The new code generators write our entire boilerplate API scaffolding automatically. I'm on track for a promotion by winter.

Same thing in auditing. The automated reconciliation scripts run four hundred ledger accounts before I finish my morning coffee. Our regional director says we'll be handling thirty percent more client volume without adding overhead.

I wish hospital management had magic software. We had forty-two admissions in ER triage today. Every executive wants to cut nursing ratios, but an algorithm can't start a pediatric IV on a dehydrated toddler with rolling veins.
Preach, Chloe. A machine doesn't calm an angry customer down when a case of wine arrives smashed on the pallet either. Human work takes human presence.
Here's to steady work, honest pay, and having Friday night with the people who matter.
Glasses clink under the soft yellow lights. In Year Zero, the future looks like a straight, reassuring line: rising careers, predictable mortgages, and weekend gatherings that never feel stolen.
Year Two. Inside the employee breakroom at Oakridge Liquors, a newly mounted digital touchscreen tablet glows with a cold, persistent blue LED ring beside the bulletin board.

Adriana, look at this. The tablet recalculated my shift. It trimmed eight minutes from yesterday, eleven minutes from today, and pushed my start time back thirty-five minutes tomorrow. I'm down to twenty-seven hours this week!

I saw the memo from district headquarters. Corporate rolled out a dynamic 'Workforce Optimization Algorithm'. It monitors register transactions per minute and trims staffing dynamically to cut wage drag.
How am I supposed to pay rent when the computer cuts my paycheck by eighty dollars every two weeks with zero warning?

I'm scheduling you for manual inventory shelf resets in the backroom, Kendra. The algorithm only tracks front registers. As long as I'm manager here, I'll protect your hours where the software can't reach.

Adriana signs the paper schedule with firm strokes of her pen. But behind her, the wall tablet chimes with an alert: 'SHIFT OVERLAP DETECTED - 14 EXCESS MINUTES IDENTIFIED.' The subtle squeeze has begun.
Tuesday morning at Pete's Auto Care. Marcus's compact sedan sits on Lift 1, draining warm synthetic oil into the rolling collector drum.
Hey Todd! Just dropping by for the 40,000-mile lube service. Still loving our company's new AI code tools. We don't even write unit tests anymore—the model does it instantly.
Sounds slick, Marcus. But who checks if the model's tests are actually catching edge cases, or just rubber-stamping its own syntax?
More importantly, Marcus—who are they hiring to replace the junior guys who leave? I saw on the morning wire that your tech firm froze all entry-level hiring across the state.

Reporting on regional commerce: mid-tier software and corporate accounting firms announced a 14% decline in entry-level hiring this quarter, citing internal generative tooling gains and reduced associate onboarding requirements.
Well... our VP said it's just a temporary pause while they restructure teams. I'm sure it'll pick back up by spring.
Tires are rotated, Marcus. Synthetic 0W-20 is fresh. Keep an eye on your bank account, man. When the people at the top stop training juniors, they're usually getting ready to prune the tree.
Late Tuesday evening. Two ceramic mugs of chamomile tea steam gently on Todd and Adriana's kitchen table beside the monthly utility statements and grocery receipts.

The scheduling algorithm shaved eighty dollars off Kendra's check this week, Todd. I had to create dummy stockroom work orders just to keep her rent money intact. It feels like wrestling a machine that doesn't blink.

Marcus came by the shop today. He's talking like everything is fine, but Pete and I saw the news. His firm froze entry-level hiring. He thinks he's indispensable because he can prompt the code generator, but he doesn't see the ceiling closing in.

We're safe in our careers, Todd. People will always need their cars fixed and their retail stores run by someone who knows how to handle people. But the margin for error for everyone else is getting razor-thin.
Then we stay disciplined. Pay off the truck note early. Keep our tools sharp, our savings stocked, and our eyes open.
Year Four. A brisk Sunday afternoon on Todd and Adriana's backyard patio. Dry autumn leaves skitter across the wooden deck as Marcus sits motionless, staring into an untouched can of soda.

They cut forty-two of us on Thursday morning. A ten-minute video call where our manager's camera was turned off. He read from a legal script about 'headcount rationalization through autonomous workflows.'

Same thing happened in my accounting division, Marcus. Our firm let go fourteen junior analysts last month. The senior partners didn't even replace them—they just run the audit automation scripts themselves.

I've submitted three hundred and twenty applications in three weeks. Every single rejection arrives within ten seconds from automated ATS screening algorithms. You can't even get a human being to read a cover letter.
Eat the sandwich Todd made, Marcus. You're not an algorithm, and you're not a line item on an executive spreadsheet. You have skills, you have dignity, and we are going to help you through this.
The corporate ladder broke, Marcus. But your hands and your brain still work. We'll find real ground.
Inside Adriana's cramped department office at Oakridge Liquors, stacks of white copy paper cover every inch of the laminate desk.
Adriana... I printed the applicant batch for that single 16-hour part-time stocker posting. There are forty-eight applications in twenty-four hours.
Let me see the top five. A former commercial copywriter with nine years of agency experience. A junior corporate paralegal. A graphic designer with an MFA.
People with ten years of professional experience fighting college kids for fifteen dollars an hour to unload bourbon boxes at six in the morning. It feels wrong, Adriana.
It is wrong, Kendra. The white-collar ladder broke, and everyone is landing on the service floor. We treat every applicant with respect, but we protect our permanent crew.
Pete's Auto Care, Bay 3. Marcus's car idles with a rough shudder, the check engine light glowing steadily amber on the instrument cluster.
Plugging the scan tool into the OBD-II port... and look at that. Screen flashes red: 'ENCRYPTED TELEMETRY GATEWAY - REQUIRES DEALER CLOUD SUBSCRIPTION TOKEN: $400/YEAR.'
Four hundred dollars just to tell me which spark plug is misfiring? Todd, I'm down to my last month of emergency savings. I can't pay a four-hundred-dollar software subscription!

Automaker lobbyists pushed the bill through the state capital last winter under the guise of 'cybersecurity'. They want to kill independent repair shops and force every working stiff into five-hundred-dollar dealer diagnostic bays.

The State Independent Automotive Alliance has filed an emergency petition, alleging automaker proprietary software paywalls constitute an unlawful anti-competitive restraint on independent mechanics and vehicle owners.

Hand me that breadboard jumper and the open-source pin bridge, Pete. We don't bow to software paywalls in this shop. We'll read the raw analog waveform directly off the crankshaft sensor with the oscilloscope.

Todd taps into the wire loom with grounded precision. The green oscilloscope wave leaps to life on the vintage CRT monitor: Cylinder 3 ignition coil breakdown. Forty-five dollars for a replacement coil, and Marcus's engine purrs like a kitten. Human craft beats the paywall.
Year Six. Wednesday mid-morning at Pete & Todd's Auto Care. Bay 2 and Bay 3 stand empty, their polished concrete floors reflecting the pale grey light of an overcast autumn sky.

County transit report came out this morning, Todd. Vehicle miles traveled down twenty-two percent across the region. Former office commuters aren't driving into the glass towers anymore—they're either remote or delivering food bags on bald tires.

Nobody does the 60,000-mile preventative transmission flushes or timing belts anymore, Pete. They wait until the belt snaps on the highway or the metal-on-metal squeal can be heard from two blocks away.

That's why we don't gouge, kid. When the big chain shops start pushing four-hundred-dollar fuel injector cleans to make up their quotas, we stick to honest diagnostics. Trust is the only commodity that doesn't depreciate.
A battered silver crossover limps into Bay 1, its front wheel wells screeching with every rotation. Elena, a gig-delivery courier, steps out holding a courier thermal bag, looking exhausted.
Todd, please tell me you can fix it today. If I'm not online for the evening rush, the delivery algorithm drops my dispatch tier. I've got two kids and rent due on the first.
Pads are down to the steel backing plate, Elena. It's scored into the front rotors. You were about three hard stops away from losing your hydraulic piston.
How much? Just... give it to me straight. The corporate chain shop down the boulevard quoted me seven hundred and fifty dollars.
I can turn the rotors on our vintage lathe instead of replacing them, and put on ceramic pads for sixty-five dollars wholesale. Labor is on the house, Elena. You keep your dispatch tier.
Todd... I don't know what to say. If it weren't for this shop, people like me couldn't survive out here.
Oakridge Liquors front concourse. Four unstaffed self-checkout kiosks flash red override beacons simultaneously, emitting high-pitched warning chimes as long lines of customers grow irritated.

Adriana! Kiosk two froze on an ID verification, kiosk four flagged a false weight error on a beer pack, and someone just walked past the sensory gate with two bottles of Scotch while I was rebooting the terminal!

Override code entered. Line cleared. Corporate replaced three trained cashiers with four unstaffed automated kiosks to save twelve dollars an hour in wages, and our inventory shrinkage spiked by four hundred percent in six months.

Retail industry earnings reports confirm nationwide rollbacks of automated self-checkout technology, with major chains reporting multi-billion dollar losses due to shrinkage, technical failure, and customer dissatisfaction.
Turns out a cold touchscreen can't look a customer in the eyes, build rapport, or protect merchandise. Human presence is the only real security.
Year Eight. Outside, an autumn rain pelts the living room window. Inside, Sam and Chloe sit around the coffee table with Todd and Adriana, reviewing county tax reassessment forms.

Look at the municipal budget breakdown. The downtown commercial real estate vacancies wiped out forty-five million in commercial property tax revenue. So what did the county commissioners do? They raised residential property assessments by nineteen percent.

And city transit cut bus lines by a third. The hospital nurse-to-patient ratio went from one-to-four up to one-to-eight. The hospital tried installing an AI telemetry monitor to replace nurses, but the false alarm rate was so high that three RNs walked out in protest.
The public infrastructure is degrading because the corporations automated away the wage base that paid the municipal taxes. Everyone in town feels the pinch.
We absorb the tax hike, we maintain our home ourselves, and we keep Marcus on his feet. We don't break.

A suburban physical therapy clinic. The smell of menthol rub and heating packs fills the clinical room. Marcus sits on an examination table wearing an elastic lumbar support brace, his face pale with pain.

Everyone online said: 'Just retrain in the trades! Learn to be an electrician!' Nobody warned me that hauling five-hundred-MCM copper feeder wire through commercial conduit at thirty-one years old would herniate an L5 disc in eight weeks.

Manual trade labor is elite physical athletics, Marcus. If your musculoskeletal system didn't spend its twenties building tendon and bone density for it, sudden heavy vocational work will blow out a lumbar disc. Biology doesn't care about career advice threads.

Don't beat yourself up, Marcus. You gave it an honest try. Now you heal up. I'm talking to the county water and power utility—they need people who understand both software logic and physical telemetry systems. That's your sweet spot.
Pete's Auto Care office. On the desk sits a heavy, glossy bound prospectus embossed with the logo of 'AutoFleet National Solutions'.

Corporate rep spent forty-five minutes in here today, Todd. Offered us three hundred thousand dollars to buy the deed, keep us on as salaried supervisors, and re-skin the shop into an automated corporate subscription hub.
Mandatory corporate cloud scanners, proprietary markups on remanufactured parts, and locking Elena out of her brakes if her app account lapses. What did you tell him, Pete?
I told him Pete's Auto Care doesn't answer to algorithms, and I threw his contract in the scrap metal bin. This shop belongs to us, Todd. Next year, your name goes on the building sign beside mine.
Year Eleven. The peak of the demographic caregiving wave. Inside the lobby of 'Shady Pines Memory Care', Todd, Adriana, and Chloe look at an intake rate card on the reception counter.

Nine thousand four hundred dollars a month. And that's just the baseline rate—medication management is an additional six hundred. And listen to that hallway: call lights chiming with not a single aide in sight.

A private equity syndicate bought this entire facility network two years ago. They laid off half the certified nursing assistants and installed infrared mattress motion sensors. When an eighty-five-year-old falls, the sensor logs the data, but there's no human there to catch them.
We're not putting your mother in here, Adriana. She raised you with love, and she comes to live with us. We have the hands, and we have the will.

Todd and Adriana's home. The ground-floor spare bedroom is filled with tools, clean lumber, and stainless steel grab bars. Pete arrives carrying an impact driver and a box of galvanized structural lag bolts.

Brought the four-inch industrial lags from the shop, Todd. When an aging parent puts their full weight on a transfer rail, drywall anchors won't hold. You drive these straight into the centerline of the fir wall studs.
Thank you, Pete. In a world full of corporate private-equity care facilities gouging families, having friends with real trade skills who show up on a Saturday is everything.
Lag driven true. Zero deflection. This room is a fortress of safety now. Let's get Mom settled in.
2:15 AM in the dark kitchen. A gentle amber nightlight illuminates a handwritten medication schedule and two warm mugs of herbal tea.
How is she resting, Addie?

Fever broke. Sleeping soundly. Todd... my shoulders ache from the lifting, and my eyes burn from the shifts. But being here with her, in our own home, giving her dignity... it's the most honest thing we've ever done.
We hold the line together, Addie. We're stronger than any economic storm they can throw at us.

Year Fourteen. 5:00 AM outside the massive regional logistics distribution terminal. Steel 55-gallon burn barrels glow fiercely orange against damp pre-dawn ground mist under blinding stadium floodlights.

Look at this line, Adriana! Over six hundred warehouse workers, retail clerks, and freight drivers! They tried imposing biometric wristbands that dock wages if pickers pause for thirty seconds to wipe sweat!
When you treat human bodies like expendable mechanical cogs, this is what happens! The whole community is standing behind this strike!

Good morning. Day four of the nationwide logistics work stoppage has halted regional freight distribution across nine states. Public polling reveals 74% bipartisan approval for statutory labor protections, biometric pacing bans, and mandatory working hour caps.
The tide is turning, folks. Next stop: the state capital.
State Senate Committee Room 304. Rich mahogany paneling, gooseneck microphones, and packed spectator benches under warm chandelier lighting.

Mr. Todd, lead diagnostic technician at Pete & Todd's Auto Care. The automotive manufacturers association claims proprietary telemetry software locks are strictly necessary to protect vehicle cybersecurity. How do you respond?

Senator Vance, with respect—cybersecurity is an excuse for extortion. When an automaker encrypts a wheel-speed sensor so an independent shop can't bleed a customer's brakes without paying a four-hundred-dollar corporate subscription, that's not cybersecurity. That is a corporate shakedown of working-class families.
A working person who buys a machine owns that machine, Senator! And any honest mechanic has the right to fix it!

The testimony of these independent technicians is compelling, and the evidence of anti-competitive lockouts is overwhelming. This committee will recommend the Right to Repair bill for immediate floor vote.
The regional Machinists and Clerks Union Hall is packed shoulder-to-shoulder with hundreds of working families watching a massive projection screen.

Breaking news from the Capitol: In a historic bipartisan 68-to-31 vote, Congress has enacted the Emergency Fair Hours and Right to Repair Act. The legislation codifies a federal 32-hour standard workweek, outlaws automated biometric pacing, and guarantees permanent independent diagnostic access for all consumer machinery.
Listen to that cheer! Todd, Adriana, Marcus—we made them listen! The human worker isn't a spreadsheet variable!
Thirty-two hours. Four days of honest work for five days of pay. Time returned to human beings.
Year Seventeen. Inside the newly renovated Oakridge Liquors breakroom. Adriana pins a crisp, cleanly formatted shift schedule to the corkboard.
Adriana... is this real? My name is on the schedule: 32 hours, full-time benefits, Friday through Sunday off?

Real as rain, Kendra. With the 32-hour standard, corporate had to expand our permanent crew by twenty-five percent to maintain full floor coverage. You're permanently promoted, with healthcare and paid leave.
I can finish my graduate degree without working myself to exhaustion. Thank you, Adriana.

Pete & Todd's Auto Care. The newly painted shop sign gleams over three humming bays. In Bay 1, Maya, a twenty-year-old vocational apprentice, holds an analog diagnostic probe under Todd's watchful eye.
Todd, the computerized scan tool said zero error codes, but look at the waveform on the oscilloscope: the signal drops two millivolts right at top dead center.

Outstanding catch, Maya. Software only sees what someone programmed it to see; your oscilloscope reads the physical truth of the sensor. You just saved that customer a thousand-dollar ECM replacement.
The generational bridge is rebuilt. Young hands learning the real craft. Can't automate that, can you?
Year Twenty. Friday afternoon at 3:15 PM—the universal weekend. Warm golden sunlight bathes the back patio deck as gentle breezes rustle the mature maple trees.

Grid telemetry is running clean. I review the regional power distributions four days a week, automated systems handle the micro-load balancing, and at three o'clock on Friday, my terminal locks. No weekend calls, no panic.
Four days of sharp auditing, three days of rest. Turns out corporate productivity actually went up when people stopped being hollowed out by 70-hour weeks.
Our hospital shifts are stable, our staffing is funded, and patient outcomes are the highest in twenty years. Human care requires human time.

Signing off for the Friday evening edition: Twenty years after the onset of the automation transition, national economic indicators show sustained equilibrium under the Human Baseline standard. Strong local wages, universal independent repair rights, and restored family hours anchor a resilient civic baseline.
We kept the engines running, Addie. Through every bump, every software lock, and every long night.
And we made it to the other side with our hands steady, our community whole, and our dignity intact.

Laughter rises above the clinking glasses as the sun settles behind the autumn trees. The world did not end in chaos, nor did it freeze into an automated machine. Through persistent labor, mutual aid, and unyielding solidarity, they reclaimed their time—and built the Human Baseline.
